title: Messaging in Python: aiokafka, confluent-kafka, Celery, dead letters, outbox and idempotence
seriesDescription: Kafka and Celery clients, tenacity, circuit breakers and timeouts. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Python messaging clients: aiokafka and confluent-kafka consumers and producers, manual commits, Celery acknowledgement and retries, dead-letter publishing, outbox relays and idempotent consumers.
source: aiokafka documentation (AIOKafkaConsumer, AIOKafkaProducer); confluent-kafka-python documentation; Celery documentation (acks_late, retry options, Redis visibility timeout); asyncpg documentation; Apache Kafka producer and consumer configs

questions.prompt: Create an AIOKafkaConsumer named consumer for topic "orders" on bootstrap server "localhost:9092" in group "billing", with auto-commit disabled and auto_offset_reset set to "earliest".

checks.label: builds an AIOKafkaConsumer on the orders topic
reads from the start for a new group

questions.model:
consumer = AIOKafkaConsumer(
    "orders",
    bootstrap_servers="localhost:9092",
    group_id="billing",
    enable_auto_commit=False,
    auto_offset_reset="earliest",
)
questions.explanation: Remember to await consumer.start() and to stop() the consumer in a finally block so the group rebalances promptly. Two groups with different group_id values each receive every record.

questions.prompt: Using aiokafka, consumer is an AIOKafkaConsumer created with enable_auto_commit=False. Write the loop that reads each record msg, awaits process(msg) and only afterwards commits the offsets.
questions.model:
async for msg in consumer:
        await process(msg)
        await consumer.commit()
questions.explanation: Commit after processing gives at-least-once: a crash between the two steps replays the record. Batch commits (commit every N records) trade duplicates for throughput. Do not forget a finally block that stops the consumer.

questions.prompt: With a started AIOKafkaProducer named producer created with acks="all", write the line that sends bytes payload to topic "orders" with key b"order-7" and waits until the broker has acknowledged it.
questions.explanation: send() returns a future after buffering; send_and_wait() also waits for the acknowledgement level set by acks. Same key means same partition, so one order stays in order. Other correct answers await the future returned by send().

questions.prompt: With a confluent_kafka Consumer named consumer already subscribed (enable.auto.commit false), write the loop that polls with a 1 second timeout, skips empty polls, calls handle(msg) and then synchronously commits that message.
questions.model:
msg = consumer.poll(1.0)
    if msg is None:
        continue
    if msg.error():
        log.error(msg.error())
        continue
    handle(msg)
    consumer.commit(message=msg, asynchronous=False)
questions.explanation: poll() returns None when nothing arrived and a message object whose error() may be set. Committing after handle() is at-least-once. The loop must also call consumer.close() on shutdown so the group rebalances quickly.

questions.prompt: Which practices keep an aiokafka consumer healthy inside an asyncio service? Select all that apply.

options.text: Offload CPU-heavy or blocking work to an executor or process pool.
options.why: Correct: the event loop must stay free to send heartbeats and fetch.

options.text: Stop the consumer in a finally block so the group rebalances promptly.
options.why: Correct: a clean stop leaves the group instead of waiting for the session timeout.

options.text: Commit only after the record has been processed successfully.
options.why: Correct: committing first gives at-most-once and can lose records.

options.text: Call time.sleep() for back-off inside the consumer coroutine.
options.why: It blocks the whole event loop, delaying heartbeats and every other task.

options.text: Create a new AIOKafkaConsumer for every message to keep state clean.
options.why: Each consumer join triggers a rebalance; reuse one long-lived consumer.

questions.explanation: Use await asyncio.sleep() for pauses, keep batches small enough to finish within max_poll_interval_ms, and handle rebalances by committing processed offsets first.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: With Celery default settings, a worker that crashes in the middle of running a task can lose that task.
questions.reason: By default Celery acknowledges the message just before the task starts executing; acks_late=True moves the ack to after completion.

whys.a: Correct: The early ack deletes the message from the broker before the work is finished, so a crash loses the task.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: acks_late=True gives at-least-once, so tasks must then be idempotent. A worker process killed by the OS (for example out of memory) also needs task_reject_on_worker_lost=True to be redelivered.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: Tasks should still be idempotent when acks_late=True is enabled.
questions.reason: acks_late=True makes Celery guarantee that every task executes exactly once.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Correct: A is true because a crash after the work but before the ack runs the task again. R is false: late acks only give at-least-once.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: Use a unique key (task id or business id) and a conditional write so the repeat has no extra effect.

questions.prompt: Declare a Celery task send_email on an app named app that acknowledges late, retries automatically on ConnectionError with exponential back-off, and gives up after 3 retries.
questions.explanation: retry_backoff=True doubles the delay each retry starting at 1 s (capped by retry_backoff_max) and retry_jitter is on by default. Combined with acks_late the task can run more than once, so make send_email idempotent.

questions.prompt: A Celery worker runs with --concurrency=4 and the default worker_prefetch_multiplier of 4. How many messages can it reserve from the broker at one time?
questions.explanation: Prefetch count = concurrency x multiplier = 4 x 4 = 16. With long tasks set the multiplier to 1 (and often acks_late) so one slow task does not hold a backlog hostage.

questions.prompt: A Celery task using a Redis broker runs for 2 hours while the broker visibility_timeout is the default of 1 hour and acks_late is on. What is the likely result?

options.text: The worker is killed after one hour, because Celery enforces the visibility timeout as a time limit.
options.why: The timeout is a broker redelivery rule, not a task time limit.

options.text: The broker redelivers the message, so the task runs twice at once.
options.why: Correct: an unacked message becomes visible again after the timeout.

options.text: The task result is lost but the task itself still runs exactly once to completion.
options.why: A duplicate run is the problem, not a lost result.

options.text: Redis extends the timeout automatically for as long as the worker stays connected.
options.why: Redis does not extend it; you must raise visibility_timeout yourself.

questions.explanation: Raise broker_transport_options["visibility_timeout"] above your longest task, or use a broker with real acknowledgement semantics. Idempotent tasks make the duplicate harmless.

questions.prompt: A consumer wraps processing with tenacity using stop_after_attempt(4) and wait_fixed(2). If every attempt fails, how many seconds does tenacity spend waiting between attempts?
questions.explanation: Four attempts have three gaps between them: 3 x 2 s = 6 s. The wait is not applied after the last failed attempt, which is re-raised or wrapped in RetryError.

questions.prompt: In an aiokafka consumer, after retries are exhausted for msg because of exception exc, write the line that publishes msg.value to the topic "orders.dlq" with a header named "error" containing the error text, waiting for the broker acknowledgement.
questions.model: await producer.send_and_wait("orders.dlq", value=msg.value, key=msg.key, headers=[("error", str(exc).encode())])
questions.explanation: Also copy the original topic, partition and offset into headers so a replay tool can find the source. Commit the original offset only after the dead-letter send succeeds, otherwise the record can be lost.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: A long CPU-bound call made directly inside an aiokafka consumer coroutine can trigger a consumer-group rebalance.
questions.reason: The heartbeat and fetch tasks run on the same asyncio event loop, so a blocked loop cannot send heartbeats in time.

whys.a: Correct: While the loop is blocked no heartbeat is sent, the session timeout expires and the coordinator removes the member.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: Run the work in loop.run_in_executor or a process pool, keep each poll batch short, and tune max_poll_interval_ms and session_timeout_ms only after fixing the blocking.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: Awaiting producer.send_and_wait() guarantees the record is stored on every replica of the partition.
questions.reason: The number of replicas that must acknowledge a write is controlled by the producer acks setting and the topic min.insync.replicas.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Correct: A is false: with acks=1 only the leader has confirmed, and with acks=all it is the in-sync replicas, not every replica. R is true.

questions.explanation: Use acks="all" with min.insync.replicas of 2 on a replication factor 3 topic for durable writes.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: Setting auto_offset_reset="earliest" makes a new consumer group read from the start of the retained log.
questions.reason: Kafka removes old log segments according to retention time or size limits.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Correct: Both are true, but retention is a different mechanism: "earliest" means the first retained offset, whatever it is.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: The setting applies only when the group has no committed offset. Once offsets exist, the group resumes from them.

questions.prompt: Match each AIOKafkaConsumer parameter with what it controls.

right.text: Consumers sharing the same value split the topic partitions between them
Whether the client commits offsets on a timer
Where to start when the group has no committed offset
Upper bound on the records returned by one getmany call
The number of broker replicas that must acknowledge a write

questions.explanation: The last distractor belongs to the producer side (acks). Keep consumer and producer settings separate when debugging.

questions.prompt: True or false: calling time.sleep(5) inside an async consumer loop pauses only the current message while the rest of the event loop keeps running.

options.why: time.sleep is a blocking call, so it freezes the whole event loop for the process.
Correct: every coroutine, including heartbeats, stalls for five seconds.

questions.explanation: Use await asyncio.sleep(5) for a non-blocking pause.

questions.prompt: With an asyncpg connection conn and a string msg_id, write the statement that inserts msg_id into processed_messages(message_id) with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING and stores the returned command tag in status. Use a positional placeholder.

checks.label: uses the $1 placeholder and passes msg_id

questions.model:
status = await conn.execute(
    "INSERT INTO processed_messages (message_id) VALUES ($1) ON CONFLICT (message_id) DO NOTHING",
    msg_id,
)
questions.explanation: asyncpg returns the command tag as text such as "INSERT 0 1" for a new row and "INSERT 0 0" for a duplicate, so status.endswith(" 0") means already seen. Run it in the same transaction as the business effect (async with conn.transaction()).

questions.prompt: In an asyncpg transaction, write the fetch that selects up to 100 unpublished rows (published_at IS NULL) from outbox in id order, locked so that several relay workers never take the same rows and do not block each other. Assign the result to rows.
questions.explanation: Publish each row, then UPDATE outbox SET published_at = now() for the ids, still inside the transaction. A crash after publishing re-sends the event, so downstream consumers must be idempotent. Several relays may reorder events of one aggregate.

questions.prompt: ledger and bank are dicts of transaction id to amount. Write def reconcile(ledger, bank, tol=0.01) returning a tuple (ids only in ledger, ids only in bank, ids in both whose amounts differ by more than tol).

checks.label: finds ids only on one side

questions.model:
only_ledger = ledger.keys() - bank.keys()
    only_bank = bank.keys() - ledger.keys()
    diff = {k for k in ledger.keys() & bank.keys() if abs(ledger[k] - bank[k]) > tol}
    return only_ledger, only_bank, diff
questions.explanation: Any loop-based version is fine. Use Decimal or integer cents for money, report all three buckets with counts and sums, and allow a grace window for late-arriving data before raising an alert.
